narrative:
The model estimated a 52.9% chance that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt. Because that placed you on the failure side of the decision, your application was denied. This is not a certainty; it means the available information put you just over the line toward predicted failure.

The strongest factor was your third-year class rank. You were in the lowest decile, while students who were accepted averaged around the sixth decile; this was the main reason the prediction moved toward failure. Your undergraduate GPA was the next most influential factor. At 3.00 it was below the accepted-student average of 3.23, but its effect actually pushed the prediction toward passing, not failing. Family income was third in influence; coming from an upper-middle-income bracket also nudged the prediction toward passing, though much less strongly.

To improve a future application, focus on strengthening the academic record most visible to admissions, especially sustained performance in later law-school coursework, and consider retaking the LSAT if you can improve your 27, which is well below the accepted average of about 37. You should also speak with admissions to understand whether additional coursework, an explanatory statement, or a later application cycle could address the committee’s concern.
